title: Character classes: one character from a set
explanation:
A **character class** in square brackets matches exactly **one** character from the set: `[xyz]` matches one of x, y, z; `[a-f]` uses a hyphen for a range; and `[a-fA-F]` combines ranges. Put `^` first to negate it: `[^,;]` matches one character that is *not* a comma or semicolon. Inside a class most special characters lose their meaning — `[.]` is a literal dot.

There are shorthand classes for the common sets:

- `\d` — a digit, same as `[0-9]`; `\D` — any non-digit.
- `\w` — a "word" character, same as `[A-Za-z0-9_]` (note the digits and underscore); `\W` — the opposite.
- `\s` — whitespace (space, tab, newline, …); `\S` — non-whitespace.
- `.` — any character except line terminators.

```js
console.log("B2 is the suite".match(/\d/)[0]);   // "2"
console.log("50%".match(/\W/)[0]);              // "%"
console.log(/[.]/.test("a.b"), /[.]/.test("ab")); // true false
```

A class always consumes one character, so `[abc]` never matches an empty string; to match several characters from the set, add a quantifier (next lesson).
keyIdeas: `[...]` matches one character from the set; `-` makes ranges.
`[^...]` (caret first) matches one character *not* in the set.
`\d \w \s` and their capitals `\D \W \S` are shorthand classes.
`.` matches any character except line terminators.

workedExample.problem: Find every character in `"Room 4B, floor -2!"` that is **not** a letter, a digit, or a space.
steps: List what is allowed: letters `A-Za-z`, digits `0-9`, and a space.
"Not in this set" is a negated class: put `^` first → `[^A-Za-z0-9 ]`.
Add the `g` flag so `match` returns every hit instead of just the first.

pitfalls: Expecting `\w` to mean letters only — it also matches digits and `_`.
Writing `^` in the middle of a class (`[a^b]`), where it is a literal caret, not a negation.
Forgetting that an unanchored class can match anywhere: `/[xyz]/` accepts `"axb"` because one character matched.

citations.quote: Character class: Matches any one of the enclosed characters. You can specify a range of characters by using a hyphen
Negated character class: Matches anything that is not enclosed in the square brackets.
Digit character class escape: Matches any digit (Arabic numeral). Equivalent to [0-9].
Matches any alphanumeric character from the basic Latin alphabet, including the underscore. Equivalent to [A-Za-z0-9_].
Wildcard: Matches any single character except line terminators
Inside a character class, the dot loses its special meaning and matches a literal dot.
